docs.description: FDUpdate DAF validation publication and update flow documentation.
docs.html:
DAF validation publication and update flow

DAF source revision 09ea5125e2a55f21bd231fd077d5cc8a7c2d7b9b adds an opt-in publish_fdupdate_validation input to its existing manual build workflow. The job runs only after the application build and persistence jobs succeed, uses the protected fdupdate-validation environment and requests id-token: write. It prepares exact publication plans locally in the job and submits a Linux x86-64 DAF application package and the checked-in BAW master firmware package to separate publisher IDs.

The validation server must register these publishers with the same exact GitHub issuer, repository fedrnv/DAF, workflow ref fedrnv/DAF/.github/workflows/daf.yml@refs/heads/main, environment fdupdate-validation, main ref, audience fdupdate-server and workflow_dispatch event:

  • daf-application: product daf, component application, target linux/x86_64.
  • daf-baw-master: product daf, component controller-firmware, target linux/baw-master.

The protected environment variable FDUPDATE_PUBLISH_URL must be a credential-free HTTPS origin. The workflow obtains its short-lived OIDC token from the GitHub runtime, submits it only in the Authorization header and unsets the shell value after both requests. Plans bind the DAF Git commit, workflow recipe digest, versions, sizes and SHA-256 artifact digests. The server signs and commits each release independently; a wrong firmware architecture such as hsd-master is outside the publisher scope.

The DAF application keeps its existing update dialogs and BAW firmware mechanism. An enrolled installation remains unable to check or download while pending. After explicit approval, the application assignment targets daf/application and the firmware assignment targets daf/controller-firmware; the BAW master identity is carried by publication compatibility/architecture metadata. Reports use the accepted application-managed flow and are idempotent.

The Linux validation foundation is installed on the dedicated server at update.fedrv.de with a trusted public TLS edge. Only the exact publisher ingestion path is public; hawkBit Management and operator boundaries remain private. Hardware acceptance requires an accessible supported BAW master controller; simulator results are not hardware evidence.

docs.title: Enrollment codes and installation identities
docs.description: FDUpdate Enrollment codes and installation identities documentation.
docs.html:
Enrollment codes and installation identities

The installation identity page in fdupdate-server-panel uses the existing security-administrator role and exact tenant/product scope. It lists installation ID, product, assigned component target, public-key fingerprint, enrollment state, creation time, last successful authenticated-seen time and revocation state. The response contains no private key, access credential, enrollment-code verifier or reusable secret.

A security administrator may issue a code for one registered product/component and an expiry from 60 seconds through 24 hours. The server generates 256 random bits, returns the lowercase hexadecimal plaintext on a one-time response page and persists only a domain-separated SHA-256 verifier plus code ID, scope, issue/expiry time and usage state. Operator and registry audit trails record issuance without plaintext.

The installation generates and retains its Ed25519 private key locally. A rate-limited enrollment submission must match the code scope and expiry. Successful consumption and creation of the pending identity commit together in the registry snapshot; it does not approve the identity or return targets or an access credential. Wrong-scope, expired, invalid and reused codes fail closed.

Revocation verifies the selected public-key fingerprint, disables the hawkBit target and removes the server-side credential hash before the audited panel action succeeds. Registry authentication then denies status/report access, and the delivery authorizer denies metadata and artifact requests. Reusing the old request with a fresh code cannot restore a revoked public-key identity.

CLI transports use enrollment-code-issue TENANT PRODUCT COMPONENT EXPIRES_UNIX, installation-list TENANT PRODUCT and the existing installation-revoke TENANT PRODUCT INSTANCE FINGERPRINT REASON operator actions.

The live /admin transport applies the authenticated session and CSRF check before calling the private device-gateway operator API. It shows the current fingerprint, state, last-seen time and repository grants, and exposes separate approve, deny, identity revoke, repository grant and repository revoke actions. The web service receives only the gateway operator token copied into its own root-owned secret directory; that token is never rendered or sent to a browser.

The panel issues the one-time plaintext through POST /admin/installations/enrollment-code. A standalone target may provision it in enrollment.code_file; FDUpdater sends it only in the protected enrollment request together with the exact component ID. The gateway atomically consumes the persistent verifier and creates a pending identity. Exact retries from that same cryptographic request remain idempotent, while a different installation, wrong component, expired code or malformed code is rejected. Approval and repository grant remain two explicit later browser actions.

Reusable installation keys

A security administrator with complete repository authority for a product can create and manage reusable installation keys on /admin. The create form records a display name, product and component scope, repository allowlist, optional expiry, and an installation limit. The limit defaults to one and accepts bounded values such as 1, 10, or 100. The generated plaintext key is returned once in a no-store response. The dashboard and gateway subsequently expose only its stable identifier and verifier-backed metadata.

Each key card shows its creator, state, expiry, used and remaining quota, current repository allowlist, and the immutable registration history. Registration rows identify the independently generated installation identity and whether it was revoked. Quota counts distinct successful registrations; an exact retry does not consume another slot, and lowering the limit never deletes historical usage.

Editing a key can rename it, change its repository allowlist, or raise or lower its quota. Disable new enrollment stops admission while preserving inherited access for existing installations. Suspend inherited update access separately removes the key's repository authority from every derived installation until an administrator restores it. Individual installation revocation remains available through the existing fingerprint-confirmed action and does not revoke sibling installations.

All installation-key actions require an authenticated security-administrator session, a valid CSRF token, and complete product repository scope. The web service checks submitted product, repository, and key identifiers against its bounded authoritative inventory before calling the private gateway routes: POST /v1/operator/installation-keys, POST /v1/operator/installation-keys/list, and POST /v1/operator/installation-keys/update.

docs.title: GitHub Actions publication
docs.html:
GitHub Actions publication

An administrator first creates the update repository in the FDUpdate administrator panel. Creation fixes a stable project key, public/private visibility, product/component scope and one exact GitHub repository, workflow reference, protected environment and allowed ref. This repository record is the publisher authority; no second deployment registration is required. The panel displays the generated publishing secret once; the server stores only its repository- and generation-bound verifier. Rotation immediately invalidates the old secret and revocation denies publication until a new generation is issued.

The publishing job requests a short-lived GitHub Actions OIDC token. FDUpdate selects the token's current key ID from GitHub's HTTPS JWKS and accepts only an RS256 signature plus exact claims for issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com, audience, repository, workflow_ref, environment, ref, commit sha and event_name=workflow_dispatch. The token lifetime is at most ten minutes. The token and its jti are never written to audit; only a SHA-256 token identifier is held for request processing.

The HTTPS request must contain x-fdupdate-project-key, x-fdupdate-publishing-secret, x-fdupdate-source-revision and x-fdupdate-publication-comment together with x-fdupdate-request-id and the OIDC bearer token. The source revision must equal the signed OIDC sha claim. The publishing secret belongs in a protected GitHub environment secret and must never be printed; project key and comment may be workflow inputs. The gateway validates the JWT header, current repository credential and exact signed GitHub identity before consuming multipart fields. The bounded canonical plan must be the first field and pass repository scope validation before the artifact field is opened. Missing, unknown, mismatched, rotated or revoked values therefore create no artifact staging.

After dual authorization, the versioned ingestion request supplies a canonical publication plan and one bounded artifact stream. The gateway permits one artifact stream at a time, bounding concurrent staging to one maximum-size artifact and releasing capacity on every response. The artifact must match the server repository and registered product, component, platform and architecture. When provenance is required, the gateway verifies its attestation before the isolated signer verifies the digest and signs the release. The publication backend prepares hawkBit state before the immutable store becomes visible. Commit failure invokes abort and removes staged and final output. The gateway journals request fingerprints, receipts and a queryable provenance record containing project, publisher, GitHub repository, exact source SHA, time, bounded comment, release and artifact hashes. An exact request-ID retry after process restart returns the original receipt; changed SHA, comment, project or plan conflicts. Corrupt state prevents startup.

Application workflows may build, package and publish only when manually started with workflow_dispatch. They do not execute FDUpdate acceptance tests. Installation enrollment credentials, hawkBit Management credentials and signing private keys never enter GitHub Actions.

Build provenance admission

Build provenance is opt-in per publisher. With no provenance configuration, or for an absent publisher entry, publication keeps the existing flow and records provenance_not_required. A required entry never downgrades: a missing, empty, malformed, untrusted or larger-than-2-MiB bundle is rejected before release signing. Supplying an attestation when policy is disabled is also rejected, so producer and server policy changes are deliberate.

The policy file has schema fdupdate/publisher-provenance-policy/v1. A required policy pins the stable numeric GitHub repository ID, the approved builder ID and the feature availability decision:


{

  "schema": "fdupdate/publisher-provenance-policy/v1",

  "policies": {

    "example-publisher": {

      "mode": "required",

      "version": "github-private-v1",

      "repository_id": 123456789,

      "builder_id": "https://github.com/actions/runner/github-hosted",

      "availability": "private_enterprise_cloud"

    }

  }

}

Allowed availability values are public_repository, private_enterprise_cloud and private_unsupported. GitHub supports attestations for public repositories on current plans, but private or internal repositories require GitHub Enterprise Cloud. private_unsupported is an explicit fail-closed decision, not a disabled policy. Obtain and review the numeric ID independently (for example, gh api repos/OWNER/REPOSITORY --jq .id); repository names alone do not survive rename and name reuse safely.

The server provenance configuration points to that policy and, when at least one supported entry is required, to a verifier configuration. FDUpdate currently accepts GitHub CLI 2.101.0 under the MIT license. Operators pin the executable path, its SHA-256, exact version, trusted-root JSONL path and SHA-256, root generation time, maximum root age and verifier timeout. The configured maximum root age cannot exceed 30 days. Startup fails if the executable/version/hash or root/hash is wrong. Every admission rechecks the root age and the pinned files' size and modification identity.

Verification is offline and fail-closed. The server invokes the pinned CLI with the supplied bundle and custom root while network proxy variables point to a closed local endpoint and credential variables are removed. It enforces the exact artifact SHA-256, SLSA provenance v1 predicate, numeric repository ID, GitHub-hosted builder, exact workflow certificate identity, source commit and ref. This supplements the product-scoped release signature; it does not prove source correctness or claim a SLSA level.

Generate a fresh combined public/private root snapshot on an online administrative machine with gh attestation trusted-root > trusted_root.jsonl, record its digest and generation time, then transfer it through the deployment's trusted configuration channel. GitHub's root metadata has no built-in expiry. Offline verification cannot know about revocations after the snapshot, and material signed after the snapshot may stop verifying after key rotation; rotate the configured snapshot deliberately and keep policy/version changes auditable.

For a required policy, multipart fields are strictly ordered: plan, artifact, attestation, with no trailing field. The attestation is the JSONL emitted by gh attestation download ARTIFACT -R OWNER/REPOSITORY. Disabled policy continues to accept exactly plan, artifact. A successful required admission stores an immutable compact receipt and retains the bundle by SHA-256 under the publication store. Exact replay, including after restart, reuses that receipt without rerunning the verifier or signer; changed artifact, bundle, root or policy conflicts. Failed signing/publication removes a newly retained bundle.

An application repository may add the following step to its existing manual-only build job. Keep the workflow trigger as workflow_dispatch, grant id-token: write, contents: read and attestations: write, and pin the action by full commit rather than a floating tag:


- name: Attest release artifact

  uses: actions/attest@1e69f48acb82d1966a394da916b4c1698aa569d6 # v4.2.2

  with:

    subject-path: dist/fdos-update.zip



- name: Download bundle for FDUpdate upload

  env:

    GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}

  run: gh attestation download dist/fdos-update.zip -R "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY"

Pass the generated sha256:*.jsonl file as the attestation multipart field in the same authenticated FDUpdate request as the exact artifact. Attestation generation and bundle download occur only inside that explicitly dispatched producer workflow; FDUpdate's verifier performs no public-network lookup.

docs.title: Open-source publication readiness
docs.html:
Open-source publication readiness

FDUpdate remains private until the owner authorizes the exact license and GitHub visibility change. Run the local baseline audit from a clean checkout:


node scripts/audit-public-readiness.mjs

gitleaks git --config .gitleaks.toml --redact --no-banner

The audit covers tracked secret/state file names, the complete locked Rust graph, contributor identities and hosted workflow triggers. Gitleaks scans the complete Git history. Its two narrow allowlists cover only immutable disposable fixtures: the FDU-089 loopback credential and a deliberately incomplete JWT used to prove rejection. A new match blocks publication and requires rotation when authenticity cannot be disproved. Never put a finding's secret value in evidence.

The 2026-10-18 inventory found 1,726 tracked files, 610 scanned commits, one human contributor identity (two author-name spellings with the same email), and four retained manual build artifacts. The GitHub repository was private and main had no branch-protection rule. Before visibility changes, enable private vulnerability reporting, publish SECURITY and contribution policies, protect main, confirm release artifacts contain only intended packages, and rerun both commands.

Repository history contains public project/source links, example.invalid-style fixtures and the operational hostname update.fedrv.de. No customer identity or private service address was found. Production configuration and credentials stay outside Git. Historical task evidence is public engineering provenance and must be reviewed as such; accepted records are immutable.

Publication decision checklist

1. Owner approves the exact license recorded in license-decision.md. 2. All FDU-158 audit findings are closed and all D008 documentation/security policies are present. 3. The D008 gate and independent review accept one exact commit. 4. Owner explicitly authorizes GitHub visibility change. Capture the repository ID, source commit, settings baseline and timestamp before changing visibility. 5. Set visibility once, verify anonymous clone/docs/license/security links, then retain the prior settings record for rollback. A visibility rollback cannot retract already downloaded history, so a secret finding always requires rotation rather than relying on making the repository private again.

docs.title: Installation Accounts
docs.html:
Installation Accounts

Installation Accounts are human download and delegated-enrollment identities. They are separate from administrator accounts, repository publishing credentials and the Ed25519 identity/credential generated for each installed software instance.

The durable account domain is owned by fdupdate-installation-accounts. IDs use UTC YYMMDDNN, where NN is the first unused sequence from 00 through 99 for that date. A day cannot create a 101st account; it fails explicitly instead of changing the identifier shape or reusing an ID.

Email login is normalized to trimmed lowercase ASCII and must be unique. The server generates a 192-bit initial password, returns it once, stores an Argon2id verifier and requires a password change. Account views, audit and Debug never contain password material. A positive installation limit is exact; None means unlimited. Repository grants contain only canonical exact project keys and do not derive authority from product or component names.

Owner administration

The authenticated /admin page contains a separate Installation Accounts section. Owner authority and a current CSRF value are required to create an account, change its exact private-repository grants or installation limit, enable or disable it, and reset its password. Public and unknown repositories are rejected as grants. A limit is either one positive integer or explicitly unlimited.

Creation and reset return a no-store page containing the Installation ID and generated password once. Later dashboards show only safe account metadata and bounded audit. Reset invalidates the prior password immediately; disablement prevents authentication immediately. Future Installation Account sessions and download or enrollment requests must re-read current enabled state and grants rather than treating their initial session projection as durable authority.

Deployment stores installation-accounts.json beside the other mutable web runtime state under the service-writable web data directory. It is not placed in the root-owned secret directory, and that directory remains read-only to the web service.

Confirmation and self-service

The owner configures one FDUpdate-private Email channel through COT. Its protected setup binds the sender account and SMTP provider configuration, while each message supplies exactly one validated Installation Account recipient. SMTP credentials pass directly from the protected owner form into COT custody; FDUpdate retains only the opaque channel identity and revision. FDUpdate never persists SMTP credentials or a recipient-specific COT resource.

New accounts remain unusable until their current email is confirmed. The Installation Account portal supports login by ID or normalized email, forced initial password change, password recovery and confirmed email replacement. Confirmation and recovery links are short-lived, single-use and replaced by a newer challenge of the same kind. Only a SHA-256 digest of each random token is stored. Passwords are never sent by email. Password recovery, email replacement, owner reset, authority changes and disablement revoke existing Installation Account sessions.

The dynamic-recipient contract uses the typed COT SDK published at revision 9f720a6ed5a68dd1fa5df5716fdf7bea57e67c0e and an isolated conforming fixture. The same immutable COT candidate is deployed on the authorized VPS and its live health probe passes. FDUpdate treats compatibility as verified only when the typed fixture, security, UI, deployment and redaction checks all pass against that exact pin; the upstream task's unrelated open lifecycle state is not a runtime compatibility signal.

Delegated software enrollment uses the account password only as transient proof. The account's current grants must cover the installation's exact requested repository set, and its optional installation limit counts distinct signed software identities. Exact retries are idempotent; successful software receives an independent installation credential. The human password is never persisted in updater or registry state.

Registration audit idempotency is bound to a domain-separated semantic attempt: the digest of the signed enrollment request, tenant/product/component scope, provenance, resolved Installation Account ID when available, software instance and exact sorted repository set. Occurrence time and outcome do not change that attempt identity; outcome remains a separate audit transition key. Consequently an exact retry produces no duplicate row, while two repository/provenance/account variations remain distinct durable attempts even when they reuse one signed software identity. Audit schema v1 records migrate deterministically to v2 from their stored request digest and redacted semantic fields. Passwords, email, request bodies, installation credentials and signed decisions are neither inputs persisted in the audit nor exposed by its query.

Private download portal

After the required password change, /installation-account projects only the account's current exact grants that are still private. Each published release lists its digest-bound artifacts. Downloads use authenticated /installation-account/downloads/{project}/{release}/{sha256} routes, support HTTP ranges, verify the stored bytes against the published digest and return a concealed 404 for public, unknown, ungranted or mismatched targets. The account session grants no administrator or publication authority.

An account can create a bearer link for one listed artifact for 1 through 30 days; the form defaults to 10 days. The plaintext HTTPS URL is shown once, while the portal inventory keeps only its non-secret grant ID, exact target, expiry and status. The same link can download the same verified bytes repeatedly until expiry or account revocation. Its owner can revoke it from the portal with the current session and CSRF token.

Every account-created link is additionally bound to its Installation Account. Redemption re-reads the current enabled account, confirmed email and exact repository grants. Removing the grant, disabling the account, losing current email confirmation, expiry, explicit revocation, or any public/private visibility transition invalidates the link immediately. A later transition back to private does not resurrect it. Other accounts cannot list or revoke the grant, even when they share repository access.

docs.title: Installation dashboard
docs.html:
Installation dashboard

Authenticated owners, fleet operators and security administrators open /admin/installations from the administration page. The dashboard only requests products backed by repositories visible to the signed-in account. Application rows carrying repository provenance are filtered again against those repository scopes.

Each installation has one card keyed by its unique instance ID. The card shows enrollment state, fingerprint, source installation-key ID, repository grants and the last server contact. Contact within 15 minutes is labelled online; older contact is labelled offline/stale; an absent timestamp is labelled never seen. These labels describe any authenticated device contact rather than device attestation.

The separate managed-updater status comes from its heartbeat. The panel displays updater version plus client-reported and server-received heartbeat times. A heartbeat received within 15 minutes is online, an older heartbeat is offline/stale, no heartbeat is never reported, and a non-approved enrollment is inactive. Liveness uses the server-received time, so a client cannot keep itself online by supplying a future clock value. A stale updater does not by itself mean that an application update failed.

Each configured application binding is visible before its first application report. Its row identifies the target, repository, platform, architecture, channel, check permission, update permission and binding revision. The last-check column keeps the client-reported and server-received check times distinct. A binding without a report shows never reported, an unknown health and no assignment.

Reported rows show the client-reported installed version, assigned version and assignment ID, local Release/Prerelease channel, last update health/error, last check and last successful update. Publication or assignment never fills the installed-version column. Historical reported state without a current binding is retained as not currently managed rather than being presented as active authority.

Changing a binding's repository, platform, architecture or channel starts a new current outcome epoch. The first report still shows its installed version and check times, but it remains unknown until that exact provenance reports an outcome; health, last-success time and diagnostics from the previous provenance stay only in bounded history and are never relabelled into another repository scope.

The q filter matches installation ID, fingerprint, enrollment state, installation key, repository, product/component, installed and updater versions, platform, architecture, channel, managed permissions, health, errors and heartbeat/check times. Results can be sorted by last contact, installation ID or enrollment state and are paged at 25 installations. Approval, revocation and grant management links return to the existing CSRF-protected controls.

The layout uses a full table at desktop width and labelled stacked cells below 600 px. All client strings are escaped before rendering, responses use Cache-Control: no-store, query input is bounded to 128 bytes and page numbers are bounded.

docs.title: Migrating FDOS to external FDUpdater
docs.description: FDUpdate Migrating FDOS to external FDUpdater documentation.
docs.html:
Migrating FDOS to external FDUpdater

FDUpdaterFdosMigration converts the strict FDOS updater v1 configuration, current/previous slot metadata and idle engine state into a separate FDUpdater state root. It never edits or removes the FDOS root and never changes a service.

Create an administrator-owned request outside both roots:


{

  "schema": 1,

  "legacy_config": "ABSOLUTE_PATH_TO_FDOS_UPDATER_CONFIG",

  "state_root": "ABSOLUTE_NEW_FDUPDATER_STATE_ROOT",

  "instance_id": "fdos-installation-1",

  "architecture": "x86_64",

  "updater_identity": "FDUpdater.service",

  "application_identity": "FDOS.application"

}

Stop FDOS_Updater, then run the explicit migration:


FDUpdaterFdosMigration migrate --request ABSOLUTE_REQUEST_JSON

The destination must not exist. The command opens and exclusively locks the existing updater.lock; a running updater or a missing lock file blocks migration without creating or modifying legacy state. The command also rejects an active transaction, unknown fields or schemas, unsupported components/platforms, inconsistent configuration, invalid trust material and any slot whose executable does not match its size and SHA-256. It builds the complete destination in a sibling temporary directory and publishes it with one non-overwriting atomic move. A rejected or interrupted migration therefore leaves both the requested destination absent and FDOS_Updater unchanged.

The package contains:

  • fdupdater-registry.json with explicit fdos/server, fdos/agent and, when

    configured, fdos/updater registrations using the original service names;

  • copied immutable current and previous executables plus their converted slot

    metadata and retained FDOS artifact-signature domain;

  • one transaction.json per target with the legacy replay cursor and failed

    sequence, but no active transaction;

  • fdos-trust.json containing only the legacy public verification keys;
  • fdos-compat.json retaining polling, CA, pause and local health-command policy;
  • fdos-migration.json, a deterministic receipt bound to the source config/state

    hashes and migrated versions.

Application data remains at its existing path. Keep the complete legacy root and FDOS_Updater service definition until FDUpdater health and rollback have been verified by the deployment procedure. Service activation belongs to the installer and is deliberately outside the conversion command.

The later FDOS repository change should remove the in-process/workspace fdos-updater dependency and stop publishing application-owned updater commands. Its installer should provision FDUpdater independently, run this migration once, then switch the existing FDOS Server and Agent service ownership only after the migration receipt and FDUpdater health pass. FDOS UI actions should call the authenticated local FDUpdater API for status, check, apply, rollback, pause, resume and diagnostics using the fdos product and existing component names. If release publication temporarily keeps the strict FDOS v1 envelope, its compatibility provider must verify the retained original bytes in the distinct FDOS signature domain before giving normalized metadata to FDUpdater. The local state migration does not authenticate or authorize a new remote release. After rollout validation, FDOS can publish the product-neutral FDUpdate envelope and remove the legacy adapter in a separately versioned migration. The rollback procedure restores the original service definitions and legacy root without converting state back or deleting the FDUpdater package.

docs.title: FDOS updater baseline inventory
docs.description: FDUpdate FDOS updater baseline inventory documentation.
docs.html:
FDOS updater baseline inventory

This inventory covers the immutable snapshot in legacy/fdos-updater/. The source is fedrnv/FDOS commit 1013672a9d667b4b65b8205dd455d67fc18d6152. The snapshot contains 53 source-derived files plus the FDUpdate-owned MIGRATION.md provenance note. Each source-derived Git blob matches that commit.

Reproduction

The imported directory is intentionally not a complete Cargo workspace. Its root manifest still names scripts/xtask, which was not imported, so invoking Cargo against legacy/fdos-updater/Cargo.toml fails while loading the workspace. Do not repair that historical snapshot.

Use a detached checkout of the exact source commit to verify both the imported blobs and the applicable updater/distribution tests:


git clone --filter=blob:none --no-checkout https://github.com/fedrnv/FDOS.git ../FDOS-baseline

git -C ../FDOS-baseline checkout --detach 1013672a9d667b4b65b8205dd455d67fc18d6152

node scripts/verify-fdos-baseline.mjs --source ../FDOS-baseline

The command requires Git, Node.js, rustup and toolchain 1.98.0. It first compares all 53 source-derived blobs, then runs this locked package set on the full source checkout: fdos-release-format, fdos-install-layout, fdos-updater, fdos-release-publisher and fdos-release-store, including all targets. Use --integrity-only when only the import check is required.

Source-to-target disposition

| Imported surface | What it proves | FDUpdate disposition | Owner task(s) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, rust-toolchain.toml | Original workspace versions and dependency closure | Evidence only. Create a smaller product-neutral active workspace and a new lockfile; do not inherit absent FDOS members. | FDU-003 | | packages/release-format/ | Bounded signed manifest, artifact identity, rollout, replay, downgrade and exact rollback rules | Extract security invariants into fdupdate-contract; replace the closed Server/Agent/Updater enum with registered product/component identifiers and retain a versioned FDOS decoder. Signing helpers stay outside runtime crates. | FDU-002, FDU-006, FDU-011, FDU-030 | | packages/install-layout/ | Checked absolute paths, OS lock, immutable hash slots and atomic current/previous pointers | Reuse behavior in the generic installation/transaction layer. Bind every path to a registered installation root and preserve previous-slot recovery. | FDU-003, FDU-004, FDU-007 | | packages/service-runtime/ | Validated service names, bounded shutdown and Windows service dispatch | Move generic primitives into lifecycle/bootstrap crates; add systemd and Windows adapters without product names. | FDU-003, FDU-008, FDU-009, FDU-012 | | packages/common/ | Redacting Secret wrapper | Extract the wrapper only if required by the new configuration/audit APIs. The FDOS crate and its otherwise unused updater dependency are obsolete. | FDU-003, FDU-010 | | packages/task-model/src/lib.rs, project_policy.rs | Canonical UUID parsing and native absolute-path rejection currently used by updater/layout | Replace these narrow dependencies with FDUpdater-owned identity/path types. Do not import the FDOS task domain. | FDU-003, FDU-004 | | packages/task-model/src/build_report.rs | Trusted build-stage receipt consumed by the offline publisher | Define a release-ingestion receipt on the server/publication boundary; it is not a client-core type. | FDU-019 | | packages/task-model/src/cockpit.rs, conversation.rs, local_operations.rs, tests/local_operations.rs | FDOS task cockpit, conversations and local coding operations | Obsolete for FDUpdater and FDUpdate Server. Preserve only as evidence; no migration. | None | | apps/updater/src/engine.rs | Transaction phases, replay cursor, apply/rollback, health rollback, recovery and self-handover orchestration | Split into product-neutral core, transaction/recovery and bootstrap modules. Retain fail-closed transitions and remove the fixed component enum. | FDU-003, FDU-006, FDU-007, FDU-008, FDU-009 | | apps/updater/src/config.rs, control.rs | Strict config, bounded health command and native service control | Replace FDOS component/service assumptions with explicit target registration and lifecycle adapters. Remote metadata must never supply commands or service authority. | FDU-004, FDU-008, FDU-027, FDU-028 | | apps/updater/src/network.rs | Pinned/public TLS, disabled proxy/redirect behavior, bounded streaming and artifact verification | Reuse as the manifest distribution provider and make hawkBit a separate provider producing the same normalized intent. | FDU-005, FDU-006 | | apps/updater/src/cli.rs, main.rs, lib.rs | Bootstrap/status/check/apply/pause/resume/rollback/recover/run command behavior | Rebuild as FDUpdater CLI/service plus authorized local API and audit. Retain command equivalence and bounded polling; add readiness, supervision, diagnostics and per-target channels. | FDU-003, FDU-010, FDU-027, FDU-028, FDU-029, FDU-030 | | apps/updater/tests/https.rs | Real loopback TLS, signature, corruption, redirect, size and timeout checks | Port as provider/security integration coverage with generic fixture products. | FDU-005, FDU-006 | | apps/updater/examples/ | Native component, release server, certificate and distribution fixtures | Generalize into reusable test fixtures. Never ship fixture keys or synthetic trust as production configuration. | FDU-003, FDU-006, FDU-008, FDU-009, FDU-013 | | apps/release-publisher/ | Offline plan validation, domain-separated signing, immutable atomic publication and bounded framed transport | Keep out of FDUpdater. Adapt relevant receipt/signing/publication behavior to FDUpdate Server ingestion; hawkBit replaces the FDOS manifest store as the primary server. | FDU-019, FDU-020, FDU-021 | | apps/release-store/** | Bounded HTTPS serving, immutable paths, cache policy and lifecycle | Compatibility/reference only. Do not make it a second production server beside hawkBit; retain only fixtures or migration serving if an accepted task requires them. | FDU-005, FDU-011, FDU-017 | | deploy/linux/component-service.py, deploy/windows/component-service.ps1 | Native identities, permissions, service receipts, install/repair/uninstall and stable host layout | Rewrite as FDUpdater packages/installers while preserving distinct identities, receipt-bound authority and retained application/recovery data. | FDU-008, FDU-009, FDU-012 | | scripts/updater-native.cjs | Native service, self-update, isolation and recovery acceptance orchestration | Port scenarios to the canonical FDUpdater CLI gate and generic fixture products. | FDU-009, FDU-012, FDU-014 | | scripts/updater-disk-exhaustion.cjs | Bounded-volume activation and recovery behavior | Port to transactional recovery coverage. | FDU-007, FDU-014 | | scripts/release-ci.cjs | Manual-only workflow and release evidence validation | Adapt to FDUpdate build/release gates; retain the workflow_dispatch-only invariant. | FDU-012, FDU-014, FDU-019 | | docs/updater.md, docs/updatable-services.md | Historical CLI, layouts, identities, recovery and runbooks | Rewrite for product-neutral names and link the original behavior as migration evidence. | FDU-010, FDU-011, FDU-012 | | Tasks/decisions/ADR-0019*.md, ADR-0020*.md, ADR-0021*.md | Accepted security, recovery and publication decisions | Preserve unchanged. New ADRs may generalize names but may not weaken signatures, isolation, atomicity or manual publication controls. | FDU-002, FDU-006, FDU-007, FDU-009, FDU-012, FDU-019 | | Tasks/items/operations/FDOS-021*/TASK.md, FDOS-022*/TASK.md, MIGRATION.md | Historical requirements and provenance | Evidence only; never treated as current FDUpdate completion evidence. | FDU-001 |

FDOS coupling that must not enter the generic core

  • The public contract has a closed Component::{Server, Agent, Updater} enum,

    FDOS-prefixed binary/service names, /opt/fdos examples and a /fdos release URL prefix.

  • One config owns one root and at most one target of each fixed component. The new

    registry must support unrelated products, multiple independently versioned components and non-overlapping validated roots.

  • CLI parsing, artifact filenames, release publication plans and service scripts

    derive authority from the fixed component enum. New remote metadata may identify a registered target but cannot add a local path, command or service name.

  • Updater readiness is a host nonce/process record. Application update readiness,

    quiescence, watchdog restart budgets and incident reporting are new contracts; they cannot be inferred from the historical health command.

  • Historical semantic versions and the FDOS manifest cursor are compatibility

    inputs. Release/prerelease policy becomes persisted per-target state and cannot permit an implicit downgrade.

Invariants retained by migration

  • Ed25519 signatures remain domain-separated and cover exact manifest/artifact

    identity; invalid signatures, hashes, replay, expiry, downgrade and incompatible updater versions fail closed.

  • Downloads, JSON, logs, commands, retries, health checks and recovery are bounded.

    HTTPS redirects and ambient proxies remain disabled where they could change the authenticated endpoint.

  • Executables remain immutable hash-addressed slots with atomic current/previous

    pointers, an OS-held mutation lock and a durable recovery journal.

  • Configuration, credentials, application data and workspaces remain outside

    executable slots. Only receipt-bound targets inside validated installation roots can be stopped or mutated.

  • Self-update keeps a stable bootstrap, fresh readiness proof, bounded handover and

    local restoration of the previous updater without depending on an application or update server.

  • Runtime services never receive release signing keys. Publication stays manually

    initiated and published artifacts remain immutable.

Verification boundary

The reproduced package suite proves the portable Windows behavior exercised by the selected Rust tests and loopback TLS fixtures. It does not prove Linux native service behavior, reboot survival, production identities, real systemd/polkit, hosted publication or production signing. Those checks remain assigned to their implementation tasks and the Epic full gate. The historical Node native scripts were inventoried but were not executed as FDU-001 acceptance because they mutate native services and require task-specific fixtures and privileges.

docs.title: FDUpdater native packages
docs.html:
FDUpdater native packages

FDUpdater packages are built offline from the two release binaries and checked-in installer sources. The builder writes deterministic .tar.gz for Linux and .zip for Windows. Every payload has a strict manifest and SHA-256 inventory. Packages contain no credential, private key, product registration, application data or pre-authorized target.

Build the native binaries and one package from the repository root:


cargo +1.98.0 build --release --locked -p fdupdater -p fdupdater-bootstrap

node scripts/package-fdupdater.mjs --platform windows --architecture x86_64 --version 0.1.0 --fdupdater target/release/FDUpdater.exe --bootstrap target/release/FDUpdaterBootstrap.exe --output dist

Use --platform linux and extensionless binary paths on Linux. Building identical inputs twice produces byte-identical archives on the same platform. Release publication must authenticate the archive separately; the embedded hashes detect damage but are not a release signature.

After extraction, run the installer from an elevated PowerShell on Windows:


./install.ps1 install

./install.ps1 status

./install.ps1 upgrade

./install.ps1 repair

./install.ps1 uninstall

Run the corresponding commands as root on a systemd Linux host:


./install.sh install

./install.sh status

./install.sh upgrade

./install.sh repair

./install.sh uninstall

Installation creates the automatic FDUpdater service under the virtual Windows service identity NT SERVICE\FDUpdater or the non-root Linux account fdupdater. The binary directory is administrator-owned and read-only to the service. Only the state directory is service-writable. The configuration directory is readable by the service and contains a placeholder-only template. Before install, an administrator must create the strict FDUpdater.json, credentials, public trust and product registrations described in runtime-operations.md. Installation fails closed when that production configuration is absent and passes its absolute path to systemd or SCM.

Upgrade stages and self-tests both binaries before stopping the service. Failure restores the prior current/previous layout and attempts to restart the prior service. Repair replaces owned binaries and service policy without changing state or configuration. Uninstall deletes the service definition and binary root while retaining configuration, state and recovery data. Application roots are never an installer argument and are never traversed. Removing retained state is a separate administrator action outside the package command.

The documented native acceptance command is the manual-only GitHub workflow FDUpdater native package acceptance (workflow_dispatch). Its Linux and Windows jobs build each archive twice and generate ephemeral signing material outside the package. They install into unique native roots, apply a signed release through the installed CLI, force and recover an interrupted transaction, verify boot-style restart, corrupt and repair the owned updater binary, upgrade it, uninstall it, and compare state, recovery and external application-data canaries. No fixture private key enters either package. The same scenarios can be run from a repository checkout on clean hosts with:


cargo +1.98.0 build --release --locked -p fdupdater --example native_fixture

sudo bash packaging/linux/native-acceptance.sh ABSOLUTE_EXPANDED_PACKAGE_ROOT "$PWD/target/release/examples/native_fixture"

powershell -File packaging/windows/native-acceptance.ps1 -PackageRoot ABSOLUTE_EXPANDED_PACKAGE_ROOT -FixtureTool "$PWD/target/release/examples/native_fixture.exe"
